intro:

For a busy pizzeria-style counter, a family taverna, or a gyro shop with a steady lunch rush, that matters. ROAL answers the phone, reads your live menu, and helps turn more calls into clean pickup tickets without changing the number your customers already use.

sections.h2: What should AI phone answering handle in a Greek takeout shop?
sections.body:
For Greek restaurant takeout, the phone host should handle the calls your team gets all day: souvlaki platters, gyro combos, rice bowls, salads, sides, and pickup timing. It should also answer the basic questions people ask before they order, like hours, address, parking, and whether a dish is on the menu.

A good setup keeps the call short and clear. The host should say things like, "Thanks for calling. I can help with pickup orders, hours, and menu questions." That makes the call feel organized right away.

Here’s the practical list to look for:
- Take items, sizes, modifiers, and notes
- Collect the caller’s name and phone number
- Quote a ready time
- Confirm the order back before ending the call
- Skip items marked sold out
- Hand allergy-sensitive questions, complaints, catering requests, and manager requests to staff with a summary

For a Greek restaurant, that means the phone host can handle common order details like "no onions," "extra tzatziki," or "replace fries with salad" without making your cashier repeat the whole ticket. ROAL is built for that kind of restaurant phone work, and it sends the order to the kitchen screen as a clean ticket.

sections.h2: How does ROAL learn a Greek menu fast?
sections.body:
Setup is simple. The owner pastes the restaurant website, Google Maps link, or just the restaurant name and city at /try. ROAL reads the menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages like the website, menu PDFs, and menu photos, then builds a phone host in about a minute.

That matters for Greek restaurants because menus are often full of set plates, combo meals, and add-ons. You do not want to type every item by hand if you can avoid it. You can also upload a menu in any format if that is easier.

Use this quick prep checklist before you test-call:
1. Make sure the menu names are written the way your staff says them on the phone.
2. Check that prices are current.
3. Confirm hours, address, and parking notes.
4. Mark sold-out items so the host will not offer them.
5. Add any common notes, like "sauce on the side" or "call on arrival."

If a question comes up that the host cannot answer, it lands in an inbox. You answer it once, and the host knows it from then on. That helps with local details like where to park, which entrance to use, or whether a holiday menu is available.

sections.h2: What does a Greek takeout call sound like?
sections.body:
Here’s a simple example of how a pickup call can go. The exact words will vary, but the flow should feel natural and quick.

"Thanks for calling. How can I help with your order today?" 

A caller might say they want one chicken souvlaki platter, one Greek salad, and a side of hummus. The host can then ask for size or modifier details, collect the name and phone number, and give a ready time.

A clean call flow for Greek takeout often looks like this:
- Greeting
- Order items
- Modifiers and notes
- Name and phone number
- Ready time
- Read-back of the full order

Worked example: say your average pickup order is $28. If your phone host takes 25 completed orders in a month, that is 25 × $0.90 = $22.50 in order fees. Plug in your own average order size and monthly call volume to see what your cost would look like.

The key point is that the host does not take card numbers over the phone. Payment happens at pickup or however your restaurant already takes payment. That keeps the process aligned with the way your team already works.

sections.h2: How do the phone and forwarding setup work?
sections.body:
You do not need to give up your existing restaurant number. When you claim the host, ROAL gives each location its own phone line automatically, and you forward your current number to it.

That can be all calls, or only when busy or unanswered. A simple setup plan is:
1. Claim the host.
2. Test-call it in the browser.
3. Choose when calls should forward.
4. Forward your existing number.
5. Test from a real phone.

For US call forwarding, codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a call. On many landlines and some carriers, *72 forwards all calls and *73 turns it off. On GSM mobile carriers, **21*number# often forwards all calls and ##21# turns it off; **61*number# often forwards unanswered calls and **67*number# often forwards busy calls. Verizon Wireless commonly uses *72 / *73, and *71 for busy/no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal.

If you want a deeper walkthrough, see [Call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes) and [How it works](/how-it-works).

sections.h2: What does this cost compared with delivery apps and monthly plans?
sections.body:

Many AI phone answering products charge a fixed monthly fee per location, often around $79 to $599, whether or not orders come in. Human answering services usually bill per minute or per call.

ROAL uses a different model: $0.90 per completed phone order, with no monthly fee, no setup fee, no per-minute fee, and no contract. Calls, questions, and test calls are unlimited and free. You are billed monthly for completed orders only.

sections.h2: What should owners check before going live?
sections.body:
Before you forward calls, make sure the basics are right. For Greek restaurants, that means the host should know your menu names, current hours, parking instructions, and anything customers often ask about delivery zones or pickup timing.

A short launch checklist helps:
- Confirm the restaurant name, address, and phone number
- Check hours for lunch, dinner, and holidays
- Review the live menu for spelling and prices
- Mark sold-out items
- Decide which calls should forward: all calls, busy calls, or unanswered calls
- Pick the host’s voice and name

The owner can also test-call the host right in the browser before going live, with no sign-up needed. That makes it easier to catch any odd menu phrasing before customers call.

If you want a few phone greeting ideas before you start, [Phone greeting templates](/tools/phone-greeting-templates) can help. And if your restaurant is in Jersey City or Hoboken, ROAL is already set up for those areas, though it works for any US restaurant.

sections.h2: When should staff still take over the call?
sections.body:
A phone host should help your team, not replace the parts of the job that need judgment. ROAL passes the call to staff with a summary when someone asks about catering, makes a complaint, needs allergy-sensitive handling, or wants a manager.

That matters in a Greek restaurant because some calls need human care. A caller may ask about sesame, dairy, gluten, or how a dish is prepared. Another may want a large party tray or have a problem with a past order. Those calls should go to staff.

Use this simple rule:
- Basic pickup order: let the host handle it
- Menu, hours, address, parking: let the host handle it
- Allergy-sensitive or upset caller: route to staff
- Catering or reservation request: route to staff or collect the request for follow-up

ROAL also lets the owner answer unknown questions once, and the host learns from that. That can reduce repeat interruptions for questions like "Do you have baklava today?" or "What time do you stop taking pickup orders?"

If you run more than one location, the menu and call history tools in the dashboard can help keep each store organized. A multi-location setup is useful when one spot is busier than the other or each location has a slightly different menu.
